recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — state the conditions each theorem needs and what each one concludes.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: State Rolle's theorem
steps.margin_note: First mark. The examiner reads for the three conditions and for the conclusion f′(c) = 0. Write the interval against each condition — closed for continuity, open for differentiability.
steps.memory_tip: Three conditions, then one conclusion. Closed interval for continuity, open interval for the derivative, equal values at the two ends.
lines: Rolle's theorem: Let f : [a, b] → ℝ be a function such that
(i) f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b)
Then there exists at least one c ∈ (a, b) such that f′(c) = 0.
Geometrically: between two points of the curve at the same height there is at least one point where the tangent is horizontal.

recall.must_convey: That Rolle's theorem needs f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b) and f(a) = f(b), and then gives at least one c in (a, b) with f′(c) = 0.

steps.why: All three conditions carry this mark together. The theorem is false if any one of them is dropped, so a statement that leaves out continuity, or gives the same interval for both conditions, is not the theorem.
common_mistakes: Writing both conditions on the same interval — continuity is on the closed [a, b], differentiability on the open (a, b).
Leaving out f(a) = f(b), which is the condition that forces the derivative to be zero.
Writing the conclusion as f(c) = 0 instead of f′(c) = 0.

steps.label: State Lagrange's mean value theorem
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) is the slope of the chord and f′(c) is the slope of the tangent, so equal slopes means the two lines are parallel.
steps.memory_tip: Lagrange has two conditions, Rolle has three. Take f(a) = f(b) away from Rolle and the 0 on the right becomes the chord slope.
lines: Lagrange's mean value theorem: Let f : [a, b] → ℝ be a function such that
(i) f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b)
Then there exists at least one c ∈ (a, b) such that f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
Geometrically: there is at least one point at which the tangent is parallel to the chord joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is the special case f(a) = f(b) of Lagrange's theorem, where the right side becomes 0

recall.must_convey: That Lagrange's theorem needs f continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), and gives c in (a, b) with f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a), with Rolle's theorem as the case f(a) = f(b).

steps.why: Lagrange's theorem drops only the third condition of Rolle's theorem and replaces the conclusion f′(c) = 0 by the chord slope. Naming that link shows the two results are one theorem, and it is the line an examiner looks for when both are asked together.
common_mistakes: Writing the quotient upside down as (b − a)/(f(b) − f(a)).
Keeping f(a) = f(b) as a condition of Lagrange's theorem, which turns it back into Rolle's theorem.
Saying the tangent is parallel to the x-axis, which is true for Rolle's theorem but not for Lagrange's.

insider_note: Two statements, and the three conditions are the marked content in each. The only difference is Rolle's extra requirement f(a) = f(b), which turns the slope into 0.
